children: At Rs 79,999, you get the latest member in the Galaxy S26 series, an 8GB+256GB configuration, a triple camera setup, 8K 30fps video (same as the S26 Ultra), Exynos 2500 chipset, 45W wired charging, IP68 protection, and a 120Hz OLED
At A Glance:
* Display: 6.7-inch Dynamic AMOLED 2X, 120Hz adaptive refresh, 1,900 nits peak brightness, Gorilla Glass Victus+ protection
* Chipset: Samsung Exynos 2500 (3nm), Xclipse 950 GPU
* Memory: 8GB RAM (LPDDR5X) with up to 8GB of virtual RAM Plus; 128GB/256GB/512GB
* Storage: UFS 4.0 storage; USB 2.0 and no DisplayPort, so no wired DeX mode.
* Rear cameras: 50MP main (OIS) + 12MP ultra-wide + 8MP telephoto with 3x optical zoom (OIS)
* Front camera: 12MP, fixed focus
* Battery: 4,900mAh with 45W wired and 15W Qi2 wireless charging
* Software: Android 17-based One UI 9, seven years of OS updates promised
* Build: Aluminium frame, Gorilla Glass Victus+ front and back, IP68 rated
* Price in India: Rs 79,999 (256GB variant)

Samsung's Fan Edition line has always played a specific role in the Galaxy S family: give enthusiasts most of the flagship experience without the flagship bill. Last year's Galaxy S25 FE pulled that off convincingly. This year, Samsung has taken the curtains off the Galaxy S26 FE, and the phone finds itself in an odd spot. It is a genuinely accomplished device on its own merits, but it arrives looking almost identical to its predecessor while asking buyers to pay noticeably more for the privilege.

In India, the Galaxy S26 FE has gone on sale in the Rs 70,000 to Rs 80,000 bracket, a segment crowded with capable rivals from Xiaomi, Vivo and Motorola. We put the phone through its paces to see whether an upgraded chipset and a fresh coat of software are enough to justify its position.
Design And Build Quality

Pick the Galaxy S26 FE up, and it feels every bit as premium as its price tag suggests. The flat aluminium frame offers a confident grip, and the glass sandwich construction (Gorilla Glass Victus+ on both the front and back) gives the phone genuine heft without tipping into unwieldy territory.
Samsung has retained a full IP68 rating, so the phone can survive accidental dunks of up to 1.5 metres for half an hour.

The most visible change from the S25 FE sits around the cameras. Where last year's sensors sat flush with the back panel, the S26 FE now houses them in a distinct, slightly raised camera island finished in a translucent material that adds a bit of visual flair without being showy.
Everything else, from the flat sides to the aggressively curved display corners, will feel instantly familiar to anyone who has used a recent Samsung flagship.

Our review unit came in Pistachio, a subtle, understated shade that photographs well and resists fingerprints better than one might expect from a glossy glass back. Blueberry and Graphite round out the colour options.

Two niggles are worth flagging. The physical buttons on the right edge sit a touch too high for comfortable one-handed reach, and the haptic motor feels noticeably weaker than what Samsung offers on the standard S26 and S26+, occasionally soft enough to miss notifications when the phone is in a pocket.

The under-display optical fingerprint sensor, by contrast, is quick and consistently accurate, even if it lacks the near-instant feel of the ultrasonic sensors found on pricier phones. Stereo speaker output is well balanced, with clear vocals and a reasonable amount of bass, though loudness has dipped slightly compared with the S25 FE in favour of a fuller soundstage.
Display
The 6.7-inch Dynamic AMOLED 2X panel is, on paper, unchanged from last year, i.e., 120Hz refresh, a 1080 x 2340 resolution, HDR10+ certification, and an advertised peak brightness of 1,900 nits.

That is not a criticism. Testing this display out in the Indian summer sun, the phone showed no major issues. However, I must mention that it turned out to be adequate in the 12PM to 1PM window when the sunlight is the most unfavourable for smartphone displays.

Two refresh-rate modes are on offer, Standard (locked to 60Hz) and Adaptive (up to 120Hz), with no 90Hz middle ground. Samsung's software is clever about dialling down the on-screen framerate when nothing is moving, which helps conserve battery without resorting to a true LTPO panel underneath. HDR10+ video support carries over from last year, though there is still no Dolby Vision, and the panel carries Widevine L1 certification so services like Netflix stream at full resolution.

Colour reproduction is vivid without veering into oversaturation, outdoor visibility is strong, and viewing angles hold up well. The one mild disappointment is the chin, which remains visibly thicker than the side and top bezels, a small inconsistency at this price point.
Performance

The headline upgrade is the move from the Exynos 2400 to the newer Exynos 2500, built on a more efficient 3nm process with a 10-core CPU arrangement (a single Cortex-X925 prime core, a mix of Cortex-A725 performance and efficiency cores, and two Cortex-A520 cores) paired with an upgraded Xclipse 950 GPU.
In benchmark testing, the gains are tangible if not spectacular. GeekBench 6 put the S26 FE's single-core score above 2,400, while AnTuTu v11 returned a score just above 2 million.

In graphics-heavy workloads, 3DMark's Wild Life Extreme stress test recorded a peak score of over 5,200, broadly in line with the previous generation's Snapdragon 8 Elite chip. Under sustained load, the chipset retained a good amount of peak performance, which is an improvement over the thermal behaviour Samsung's own S25 FE displayed before a late software fix.

Real-world performance is fluid for the most part, though occasional stutters and delayed app responses do crop up, likely a consequence of Samsung pairing this chipset with only 8GB of RAM across every storage tier, with no 12GB option (an early retail listing suggesting otherwise appears to have been an error).
Samsung's RAM Plus feature can borrow up to 8GB of storage as virtual memory to compensate, but background apps still close more aggressively than one might like at this price.

I must mention that the Exynos 2500, regardless of its 3nm architecture and Xclipse 950 GPU, is not a great fit for high-performance mobile gaming. Even gacha games like Wuthering Waves and ZZZ at times crashed due to what seemed to be demanding graphics.
Software: Good User Interface Saves The Day As Always
On the software side, the S26 FE ships with One UI 9 on Android 17 and Samsung's promise of seven major OS updates, matching the standard S26 series.
One thing that the S26 FE can flex about is that it gets Android 17 before the Galaxy S27 is even out in the markets.

The interface itself is a refinement rather than a reinvention: tidier Quick Toggle sliders, a decluttered Galaxy AI menu, and a new Warranty and Care hub that centralises device support and troubleshooting.

Samsung Health has been rebuilt with a new interface, and Now Brief gains customisable, AI-generated cards (currently capped at three) pulling from weather, health and video sources, though the results can be hit-or-miss; our card built around Samsung-related videos included at least one unrelated Google Pixel clip.

Other additions include My FanCam, an AI tool that tracks a chosen subject in a video and keeps them centred through re-framing, Driving Report for logging car journeys, expanded frame-rate options in the Pro camera mode, and Bixby widgets bolstered by Perplexity integration, with the option to set Perplexity as the default assistant.
Cameras: A Triple Camera Unit
The Galaxy S26 FE carries over the exact same camera hardware as its predecessor:
* a 50MP Samsung ISOCELL GN3 main sensor with optical image stabilisation,
* a fixed-focus 12MP ultra-wide,
* and an 8MP telephoto offering 3x optical zoom, also with OIS.
* The front camera is a fixed-focus 12MP unit with a greater FOV.

Daylight photography from the main sensor is genuinely impressive, with strong detail, accurate white balance and pleasant, natural-looking colours, both at the native focal length and at 2x zoom, which doubles as a serviceable close-up option.

The telephoto camera performs better than its modest 8MP resolution suggests in good light, though detail softens noticeably indoors. The ultra-wide camera's biggest limitation is its lack of autofocus, ruling out close subjects, but colours and white balance remain consistent with the main sensor.

Low light is where the compromises show. Default output from the main camera is fairly flat, and while Night mode helps with noise and contrast, it needs to be manually re-enabled through Samsung's Camera Assistant add-on rather than working automatically.

The telephoto camera in particular struggles after dark, producing soft, noisy results even with Night mode engaged. Selfies remain a strength across the board, with sharp detail and reliably accurate skin tones.

Video capabilities are solid rather than spectacular: the main camera tops out at 8K at 30fps or 4K at 60fps, while the ultra-wide and telephoto are limited to 4K at 30fps. Stabilisation is a genuine highlight, staying smooth across all three rear cameras during both stationary shots and walking footage.
A slow motion mode is also available that shoots at 120fps.
Battery Life And Charging
The 4,900mAh cell is unchanged from the S25 FE, and Samsung has stuck with conventional lithium-ion chemistry rather than the silicon-carbon cells rumoured ahead of the phone's debut.

Even so, the more efficient chipset appears to translate into meaningfully better endurance. Roughly 15 hours of average daily run time, without any change in battery capacity. In terms of everyday heavy use, with a mix of messaging, streaming, browsing and social media, the phone comfortably lasts a full day with some charge to spare.

Charging speed remains the phone's weakest link relative to the competition. The Galaxy S26 FE supports 45W wired charging, and testing found it capable of reaching 69 per cent in 30 minutes and a full charge in roughly an hour and 35 minutes when paired with a compatible PPS charger.

That is a marginal improvement over the S25 FE, but rivals in the same price bracket, several offering 90W or faster charging with larger batteries, comfortably outpace it. Wireless charging tops out at 15W over Qi2, and the phone also supports reverse wireless charging. Battery health options are basic: a straightforward 95 per cent charge limit toggle, or a custom cap, with no built-in bypass charging.
Connectivity

The Galaxy S26 FE is a dual-SIM 5G phone with eSIM support, though only two connections can be active simultaneously. Positioning support covers GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou, and the phone includes Wi-Fi 6e (tri-band availability varies by region), Bluetooth 5.4 and NFC.
There is no FM radio, no 3.5mm headphone jack, no IR blaster, and notably no UWB support.

One genuine step backwards is the USB-C port, which has been downgraded to USB 2.0 data speeds from the USB 3.2 Gen 1 found on the S25 FE, and the phone has also dropped DisplayPort video output over USB-C, leaving only wireless Samsung DeX for a desktop-style experience.
It is a small but real cut for a phone at this price.
What Stood Out?
* Premium, IP68-rated build with a genuinely useful colour option in Pistachio
* Bright, vibrant 120Hz display with strong outdoor visibility
* Noticeably improved battery efficiency without a capacity increase
* Polished One UI 9 software backed by seven years of OS updates
* Strong daylight photography and excellent video stabilisation
What Could Have Been Better?
* Camera performance dips in low light, especially on the telephoto lens
* Weak haptic feedback compared with the standard S26 series
* 45W charging trails rivals offering faster speeds and bigger batteries
* USB-C port downgraded to USB 2.0, with DisplayPort output dropped entirely
* Price increase is hard to justify given how little has changed since the S25 FE
Verdict: Should You Buy The Samsung Galaxy S26 FE?

Not everyone is convinced the S26 FE earns its higher price. In a widely discussed opinion piece, Tech Advisor's Anyron Copeman argued that Samsung would have been better served skipping a year altogether, pointing out that beyond the new chipset, the changes over the S25 FE amount to little more than a refreshed ultra-wide sensor and One UI features that are not exclusive to the FE line anyway. His recommendation for most buyers: pick up a discounted S25 FE instead.

Having spent time with the S26 FE, we would not go quite that far. The performance gains are real, if modest, and this year's phone is thermally better behaved than the S25 FE was at debut. But it is hard to disagree with the broader point: this is an iterative update wearing a higher price tag, and buyers who already own an S25 FE, or who are happy to shop last year's model at a discount, are unlikely to feel like they are missing much.

The Samsung Galaxy S26 FE remains one of the more complete mid-range flagships on the market: the build quality is excellent, the display is bright and vibrant, the main camera holds its own in daylight, and One UI 9 brings genuine software polish along with an industry-leading update promise. Where it stumbles is in the details that matter most at this price: charging speed lags the competition, low-light camera performance is inconsistent, RAM feels stretched at 8GB, and the USB-C downgrade is a curious step back.

None of these is a dealbreaker individually. Together, though, alongside a price hike over a phone that changed very little, they make the Galaxy S26 FE a harder recommendation than it needs to be. It is a very good phone, so let's get that out of the question. It is simply a less compelling upgrade than Samsung's FE line has trained buyers to expect. At this price, my frugal mind is telling me to go for the Galaxy S25 FE instead, which offers more or less the same performance as the S25 FE but is also available at a much better price.  At the time of publishing this review, the S25 FE is costing Rs 58,999 for the 8+128GB configuration and Rs 66,499 for the 12+256GB configuration.
That said, the S26 FE is a beautifully stacked device, and the new 2nm Exynos 2500 is a good chip to possess, if, and that is a huge if, you have the budget for it.
